name: TypeScript
description: TypeScript is JavaScript with types: it catches mistakes while you write code, before the program runs.

blocks.html:
Introduction & Setup

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Why TypeScript?

JavaScript is flexible, but that flexibility can hurt. You can pass a number where a string is expected, mistype a property name, or call a function with the wrong arguments. JavaScript will not complain. The program simply breaks later, often when a real user is using it.

TypeScript is JavaScript with types. You add small labels that say what kind of value each variable or function should use. A tool called the compiler reads your code and shows mistakes while you write, before the program runs. TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript, so every valid JavaScript file is also valid TypeScript. You can learn it step by step.

Browsers and Node.js cannot run TypeScript directly. The compiler first removes the types and writes normal JavaScript. That JavaScript is what actually runs.

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Installing TypeScript

You need Node.js and npm. Then create a project folder and install TypeScript as a development tool. The flag -D means it is only needed while you develop.

mkdir hello-ts
cd hello-ts
npm init -y
npm install -D typescript
npx tsc --version

The command tsc is the TypeScript compiler. The last line prints the installed version number.

Your first file

TypeScript files end with .ts. In the code below, : string and : number are type annotations. Press Run demo to see what the compiled JavaScript prints.

To compile the file, run npx tsc hello.ts. The compiler creates hello.js with the types removed. Then run it with node hello.js.

The compiler finds mistakes

Here is the real value of TypeScript. The variable below is declared as a number, but we try to store text in it. The compiler refuses. The output below is the real error message from tsc for a file called demo.ts, so it is a compile error and not program output. The numbers (2,1) mean line 2, column 1.

blocks.code:
let score: number = 10;
score = "ten";
blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(2,1): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

blocks.html:
tsconfig.json basics

A real project uses a settings file named tsconfig.json. Create it with npx tsc --init. After that, running just npx tsc compiles every file in the project. Here are the most common options.

OptionMeaning
targetWhich JavaScript version to produce, such as ES2020
moduleWhich module system the output uses, such as commonjs
strictTurns on all the strict checks (recommended)
outDirFolder where the compiled .js files go
rootDirFolder where your .ts source files live
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

Common mistakes

  • Trying to run a .ts file with node directly. Compile it first.
  • Editing the generated .js file. Always edit the .ts file, because the compiler will overwrite the .js.
  • Leaving strict off. It hides many mistakes that TypeScript could catch for you.
  • Thinking types exist at run time. They are removed when the code is compiled.

Key Points

  • TypeScript is JavaScript plus types, checked before the program runs.
  • Install it with npm install -D typescript and compile with tsc.
  • The compiler removes the types and writes plain JavaScript.
  • tsconfig.json controls the target, strictness and folders.

Basic Types

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Primitive types

A type annotation goes after the variable name with a colon. The three most common basic types are string for text, number for all numbers (whole or decimal) and boolean for true or false. Use lowercase names. Capital names such as String refer to different objects and are not what you want.

Type inference

You do not have to write a type every time. When you give a variable a starting value, TypeScript infers (works out) the type for you. After that the type is fixed. Good TypeScript style is to let inference work for simple variables and write annotations where the type is not obvious, such as function parameters.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(3,1): error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.

blocks.html:
The output above is a compile error from tsc. TypeScript inferred that city is a string from its first value, so storing a number is not allowed.

Arrays and tuples

An array holds many values of the same type. Write the item type followed by [], for example number[]. You can also write Array<number>. A tuple is an array with a fixed length where each position has its own type.

any versus unknown

Sometimes you do not know a type, for example data from outside your program. TypeScript gives two choices. The type any turns off checking, so anything is allowed and mistakes come back. The type unknown means "could be anything", but you must check the type before you use the value. Prefer unknown.

TypeCan hold any value?Safe to use directly?
anyYesYes, but no checking at all
unknownYesNo, you must check it first

blocks.output:
text of length 5
number 42.0
something else

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Using String or Number (capital letters) instead of string and number.
  • Using any everywhere. It makes TypeScript act like plain JavaScript.
  • Writing an annotation that is longer than needed, such as const n: number = 5. Inference already knows it.
  • Forgetting that a tuple has a fixed length and fixed types.

Key Points

  • Basic types are string, number and boolean.
  • Arrays use type[]; tuples fix both length and the type at each position.
  • TypeScript infers types from starting values, and the inferred type stays fixed.
  • Choose unknown over any, and check it before use.

Typing Functions

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Parameter and return types

Functions are where types help the most. You write a type for each parameter, and a type for the value the function returns after the closing bracket. If someone calls the function with the wrong kind of value, the compiler tells them at once.

TypeScript can often infer the return type, but writing it is a good habit. It also protects you if you change the body by mistake.

Optional and default parameters

In JavaScript, every parameter is optional. In TypeScript, every parameter is required unless you say otherwise. Add ? after the name to make a parameter optional. Its type then also includes undefined. Or give it a default value with =, and the type is inferred.

Calling with wrong arguments

Now see what the compiler says when a call does not match. The output is a real tsc compile error for demo.ts, not program output. The function expects a number but receives text.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(5,20): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

blocks.html:
void and never

Some functions do not return a value. Their return type is void. Other functions never finish normally, for example a function that always throws an error. Their return type is never.

TypeMeaningExample
voidReturns nothing usefulA function that only prints
neverNever returns normallyA function that always throws

blocks.output:
LOG: Server started
Caught: Something went wrong

blocks.html:
Common mistakes

  • Calling a function with too few or too many arguments. TypeScript counts them.
  • Putting an optional parameter before a required one. Optional parameters must come last.
  • Mixing up void and never. A normal function that just does not return anything is void.
  • Forgetting a return in a function that promises a number.

Key Points

  • Write parameter types after each name and the return type after the brackets.
  • Use ? for an optional parameter, or = for a default value.
  • void means no useful return value; never means the function never returns.
  • Wrong arguments are reported by the compiler before the code runs.

Interfaces & Type Aliases

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Describing the shape of an object

Real programs use objects with several properties, such as a student with a name, a roll number and a grade. An interface describes the shape of such an object: which property names it must have and what type each one is. Any object with that shape is accepted, and an object with a missing or wrong property is rejected.

Optional and readonly properties

Add ? after a property name to make it optional. Add readonly before a name so it can be set when the object is created but never changed afterwards. This is useful for ids.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(9,4): error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'code' because it is a read-only property.

blocks.html:
The output above is a compile error from tsc. Changing title is fine, but code is readonly, so the compiler stops us.

Type aliases

A type alias gives a name to any type using the type keyword. It can name an object shape, but also a union, a tuple or a simple type. Use it to avoid repeating a long type.

interface or type?

For object shapes both work and look almost the same. The main differences are small. A simple rule for beginners: use interface for object shapes and classes, and use type for unions and other kinds of types.

Featureinterfacetype
Describe an object shapeYesYes
Extend another oneextendsUse & (intersection)
Name a union such as string | numberNoYes
Can be declared twice and mergedYesNo

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting a required property. The compiler will list the missing one.
  • Adding an extra property when writing an object directly. TypeScript flags unknown properties in object literals.
  • Thinking readonly works at run time. It is checked only by the compiler.
  • Using , or ; inconsistently. Either is allowed, but pick one style.

Key Points

  • An interface or type alias describes the shape of an object.
  • ? makes a property optional; readonly blocks changes after creation.
  • Interfaces use extends; type aliases combine with &.
  • Use type for unions, tuples and other non-object types.

Union Types & Narrowing

Union types

Sometimes a value can be one of several types. A union type joins types with the | symbol and is read as "or". For example, string | number means the value is a string or a number. A literal type is even more exact: it allows only specific values, such as "yes" or "no".

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

The problem with unions

With a union you can only use what is safe for every member. A number has no toUpperCase method, so TypeScript will not allow it on string | number. The output below is a real compile error from tsc.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(2,16): error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'.

blocks.html:
Narrowing with typeof and in

Narrowing means checking a value so TypeScript knows its exact type inside a block. Two common checks are typeof for simple types and the in operator, which tests whether an object has a property.

Discriminated unions

A discriminated union is a union of object types that all share one property with a literal value, often called kind. Checking that one property tells TypeScript which member you have, so you get the right properties safely. A switch on it is very clear.

Common mistakes

  • Using a method on a union without narrowing first.
  • Writing typeof x === "String" with a capital. The result is always lowercase, such as "string".
  • Forgetting a case in a switch over a discriminated union.
  • Using different property names for the tag in each member. The shared property must have the same name.

Key Points

  • A | B means the value is A or B; literal types allow only exact values.
  • Narrow a union with typeof, in or equality checks.
  • Inside the checked block, TypeScript knows the exact type.
  • A shared literal property (such as kind) makes a discriminated union easy to handle.

Classes & Access Modifiers

Classes with types

TypeScript classes look like JavaScript classes, but every property has a type and you can control who is allowed to use it. This is called access control. It helps you hide the inside of a class so other code uses it the safe way.

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">
ModifierWho can use it
publicAnyone (this is the default)
privateOnly code inside the same class
protectedThe class and its subclasses
readonlyCan be set once (in the constructor) and never changed

Private is checked by the compiler

If code outside the class touches a private member, the compiler reports an error. The output below is a real tsc compile error, not program output.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(6,15): error TS2341: Property 'cash' is private and only accessible within class 'Wallet'.

blocks.html:
Parameter properties

Writing a field, a constructor parameter and an assignment for every property is repetitive. TypeScript has a shortcut called parameter properties. If you put an access modifier in front of a constructor parameter, TypeScript creates the property and assigns it for you.

blocks.output:
Sadia teaches Databases
Sadia leads Databases

blocks.html:
Implementing an interface

A class can promise to follow an interface using implements. The compiler then checks that the class really has every required member. This is useful when many classes must offer the same methods.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking private hides data at run time. It is only a compile-time check.
  • Forgetting the access modifier on a constructor parameter, so no property is created.
  • Trying to change a readonly property outside the constructor.
  • Confusing extends (inherit from one class) with implements (follow an interface).

Key Points

  • public, private and protected control who can use a member.
  • readonly allows a value to be set only once.
  • Parameter properties create and assign fields from the constructor.
  • implements makes the compiler check a class against an interface.

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Generics

Why generics?

Imagine a function that returns the first item of an array. You could write it for numbers, then again for strings, then again for students. Or you could use any, but then you lose type safety. Generics solve this. A generic function uses a type parameter, usually named T, as a placeholder. The real type is filled in when the function is used.

TypeScript works out T from the argument. For the first call T is number, and for the second it is string. The result keeps the right type. You can also write it yourself, for example first<string>(["a"]).

Constraints with extends

Sometimes T cannot be just anything. If the function uses .length, then T must have a length. Use extends to set that rule. This is called a constraint.

The compiler checks the constraint

A number has no length, so it breaks the rule. The output below is the real tsc compile error.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(5,18): error TS2345: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type '{ length: number; }'.

blocks.html:
Generic interfaces and classes

Interfaces, type aliases and classes can also take type parameters. A very common example is a box, a list or an API response that can hold any one kind of data.

Common mistakes

  • Using any when a generic would keep the type.
  • Using properties of T without a constraint. The compiler does not know what T has.
  • Naming many type parameters without need. One letter such as T is fine for simple cases.
  • Forgetting that generics also disappear after compiling, like all types.

Key Points

  • A type parameter such as T is a placeholder for a real type.
  • TypeScript usually infers T from the arguments.
  • T extends Something limits which types are allowed.
  • Interfaces and classes can be generic, for example Box<number>.

Utility Types & Modules

" title="YouTube video player" width="650">

Utility types

TypeScript includes ready-made helpers called utility types. They build a new type from an existing one, so you do not copy and paste shapes. Here are the most useful ones. Assume T is an object type.

UtilityWhat it does
Partial<T>Makes every property optional
Pick<T, "a" | "b">Keeps only the listed properties
Omit<T, "a">Removes the listed properties
Readonly<T>Makes every property read-only
Record<K, V>An object with keys of type K and values of type V

Notice that Partial is great for update functions, where only some fields are sent. Record is a neat way to type a dictionary.

Readonly in action

A Readonly object cannot be changed. The output below is a real tsc compile error.

blocks.output:
Compile error (tsc):
demo.ts(6,3): error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'theme' because it is a read-only property.

blocks.html:
Modules: import and export

Real projects are split into many files. In TypeScript, any file that has a top-level import or export is a module. Use export to share something and import to use it in another file. You can export types and interfaces as well as values.

// math.ts
export interface Result {
  value: number;
}

export function add(a: number, b: number): Result {
  return { value: a + b };
}

export default function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a * b;
}

// main.ts
import multiply, { add, Result } from "./math";

const r: Result = add(2, 3);
console.log(r.value, multiply(2, 3));

Names inside braces are named exports. The one without braces is the default export, and a file can have only one. In the import path, leave out the .ts ending.

Enums basics

An enum gives names to a fixed set of values. A numeric enum starts counting at 0. A string enum uses text values you choose and is easier to read when printed.

Common mistakes

  • Using Partial when a value is really required. The compiler will no longer check it.
  • Forgetting that Readonly and readonly are checked only by the compiler.
  • Writing two default exports in one file.
  • Forgetting export, then wondering why another file cannot import the name.

Key Points

  • Partial, Pick, Omit, Readonly and Record build new types from old ones.
  • A file with import or export is a module.
  • Named exports use braces; a default export does not.
  • Enums name a fixed set of values; numeric enums start at 0.
